raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive, life-threatening infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrils within myocardial tissue [1,2]. Although numerous proteins can form amyloid systemically, cardiac involvement is primarily driven by two precursor proteins: monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains in light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, and transthyretin (TTR) in transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) [1,3]. ATTR is further classified into wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an age-related condition predominantly affecting elderly men, and hereditary variant ATTR (ATTRv), caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [1,4,5]. CA is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), with ATTRwt identified in up to 13% of hospitalized HFpEF cohorts [6,7]. Given the growing prevalence and the advent of disease-modifying therapies, early clinical recognition has become a major focus of international societal guidelines [3,4,8].

### Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation
The accumulation of amyloid fibrils in the myocardial extracellular space restricts ventricular filling, leading to a classic restrictive physiology with severe diastolic dysfunction [1,2]. In AL amyloidosis, circulating monoclonal light chains also exert direct, rapid proteotoxic damage on cardiomyocytes, compounding mechanical dysfunction [1,9]. Clinically, patients present with progressive heart failure symptoms, conduction disease, and low-output states [1,9]. Crucial systemic "red flags" that raise suspicion for ATTR include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and autonomic neuropathy [4,10]. Untreated CA has an extremely poor prognosis, with median survival ranging from less than six months in advanced AL to three years in ATTR [2,11].

### Diagnostic Evaluation
Electrocardiography often shows low QRS voltage or pseudoinfarct patterns, though voltage-to-mass mismatch is highly variable, especially in ATTR [8,10]. Echocardiography typically demonstrates concentric ventricular thickening, biatrial enlargement, and relative apical sparing of global longitudinal strain [12]. 

Myocardial tissue characterization has been revolutionized by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging and nuclear bone scintigraphy. CMR detects diffuse late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and provides quantitative measurements of native T1 and extracellular volume (ECV) fraction, both of which serve as highly sensitive diagnostic and prognostic markers [2,13]. Meanwhile, bone scintigraphy using technetium-labeled tracers ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-PYP or DPD) has enabled a reliable non-invasive diagnostic pathway [14,15]. According to multi-societal consensus guidelines, a grade 2 or 3 myocardial tracer uptake on bone scintigraphy, in the verified absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia (confirmed via normal serum/urine immunofixation and free light chain assay), is 100% specific for ATTR-CA, eliminating the need for endomyocardial biopsy [14,16].

### Therapeutic Advances
Management of AL amyloidosis is a hematological emergency focused on rapid clonal suppression [3,17]. Prognosis is staged using cardiac biomarkers and serum free light chains [17]. First-line therapy now consists of daratumumab (a CD38-targeting monoclonal antibody) combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD), which has significantly improved hematological and organ response rates [18].

For ATTR-CA, therapeutic strategies target the production or stability of TTR [1,4]. Tafamidis, a small-molecule TTR stabilizer, prevents tetramer dissociation into amyloidogenic monomers [19]. In the ATTR-ACT trial, tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations [19]. Acoramidis, a novel high-affinity stabilizer, has also shown significant efficacy in the ATTRibute-CM trial [20]. 

Alternatively, genetic "silencers" reduce TTR production at the hepatic level. These include the small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) patisiran [21,22] and vutrisiran [23,24], and the antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) inotersen [25] and eplontersen [26]. Originally approved for ATTRv polyneuropathy [21,23,25,26], these therapies have shown powerful cardiac benefits. Crucially, the phase 3 HELIOS-B trial demonstrated that vutrisiran significantly reduced all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR-CA [24]. Conventional heart failure therapies are generally poorly tolerated in CA, though mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists may offer a modest survival benefit [27].

### Future Horizons
Innovative therapeutics are currently targeting the active clearance of existing amyloid deposits. The recombinant human monoclonal antibody NI006 has shown promising phase 1 results, demonstrating depletion of cardiac ATTR amyloid burden on scintigraphy and CMR [28]. Furthermore, single-dose in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing using nexiguran ziclumeran (nex-z) has demonstrated rapid, deep, and durable knockdown of serum TTR [29,30], opening the door to a potentially curative, one-time treatment paradigm.
